catalog_quote: Arbore has all the features typical of the phonologies of East Cushitic languages. The characteristic three-term stop series is strongly in evidence. There is the usual system of five vowels. There are the customary rigid constraints on segmental distribution, which provide one source for the fairly elaborate sets of morpheme alternations found throughout the group. Both consonantal and vocalic length are phonologically significant. There is also the expected two-term accentual system, one characteristic of which is that it has a greater degree of significance in grammar than in lexis. The ways in which the details of Arbore phonology exemplify these general features will be very apparent in the present chapter.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Arbore has a two-term (accented vs. unaccented) accentual system of the East Cushitic tonal-accent type; the accent is primarily grammatical (morphosyntactically determined) rather than lexically contrastive. The source excerpt does not state the position of the accent in the word; the placement rule is in the unexcerpted accent section of Hayward 1984.
new_statements.domain_note: General characterization of the word-level accentual system in the chapter introduction; Hayward's transcription marks accent with acute on vowels (e.g. gaabbá 'younger sibling', hakkó 'egg', kollá 'leaf, wing' on pp. 51, 57). The section that states where the accent falls and its grammatical functions comes later in Chapter Two and is not in the open excerpt.
new_statements.identity_note: Hayward 1984 describes the Arbore spoken at Gondorobba (Ethiopian administrative name Irbore) by informants of the Marle and Gondorobba divisions (last informant 1982); no dialect split is given a separate glottocode. Glottolog alternative names: Arbora, Arborie, Erbore, Irbore; ethnonym also Hor. WALS code 'abo'.

tone_statements.citation: Mous, Maarten. 2021. The grammatical primacy of tone in Cushitic. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 62(1): 91-106. DOI 10.5842/62-0-898. (Crossref/ResearchGate metadata title: 'The Typology of Tone and Cushitic'; SciELO SA lists it under SPiL Plus vol. 62, 2022.)
tone_statements.quote: For many Cushitic languages, there is no obligatoriness of one stressed (or high-toned) syllable per word. Hyman (2006) argues that such languages are not stress languages but tone languages, where providing prominence is realised by pitch. This is at least valid for Somali, 'Afar, all of Southern Cushitic, Arbore, Konso, Oromo, Awngi, and Bilin. In the Southern Cushitic languages, the majority of the nouns are toneless and only receive tone through suffixation of high-toned morphemes - see Mous (1993: 21) for Iraqw, Harvey (2018: 76-79) for Gorwaa, Mous (2016: 21) for Alagwa, and Kießling (1994: 25-28) for Burunge. Hayward (1984: 98) notes the same for Arbore.
tone_statements.locator: Section 3 'Properties of Cushitic grammar-only tone languages', opening paragraph; Arbore also in 3.1 (culminativity, ex. 7b), 3.2 (ex. 8) and 3.3 (possessive-suffix H deletion).
tone_statements.summary: Arbore is a grammar-only (restricted) tone language: privative H vs. no tone, almost no lexical tone contrast, tone assigned and manipulated by morphology (verbal paradigms, possessive suffixes deleting a preceding H), not a stress language.
